title: Fuchs Endothelial Corneal Dystrophy (FECD): The Comprehensive Resident's Guide
summary: Fuchs Endothelial Corneal Dystrophy is a progressive, bilateral condition characterized by the loss of corneal endothelial cells and the formation of Descemet membrane excrescences (guttae), leading to corneal edema and vision loss. It is the leading indication for corneal transplantation worldwide.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: FECD is a primary dystrophy of the corneal endothelium. It is characterized by progressive cell depletion, basement membrane thickening, and the deposition of focal excrescences known as guttae. The condition eventually results in the failure of the endothelial pump-leak mechanism, leading to stromal and epithelial edema, pain from ruptured bullae, and significant visual impairment.

branches: TCF4 Gene: CTG trinucleotide repeat expansion (>40 repeats)

sections.title: Clinical Presentation & Symptoms
content: Early: Asymptomatic or mild glare/halos at night
Morning Blur: Vision worse upon awakening (due to lack of evaporation overnight)
Diurnal Variation: Vision improves as the day progresses
Pain/Photophobia: Occurs with ruptured epithelial bullae
Reduced Contrast Sensitivity
Episodic 'foggy' vision during high humidity

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Slit-Lamp: 'Beaten Metal' appearance of posterior cornea (Guttae)
Pigment dusting on the endothelium
Descemet's Membrane folds (Striae)
Stromal Thickening / Pachymetry >640 microns
Microcystic epithelial edema and bullae
Subepithelial haze or connective tissue scarring

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Imaging
content: Step 1: Ultrasound Pachymetry (Measure central corneal thickness; >640μm is suspicious)
Step 2: Specular Microscopy (Analyze Cell Density, Hexagonality, and Coefficient of Variation)
Step 3: Anterior Segment OCT (Assess for epithelial/stromal edema and Descemet's integrity)
Step 4: Scheimpflug Imaging (Pentacam) (Check posterior elevation and 'Pachy-map' for early thinning disappearance)
Step 5: Confocal Microscopy (Visualizes guttae and cell morphology when edema prevents specular microscopy)

rows: History of cataract surgery, no guttae

sections.title: Medical Management Protocol
content: Hypertonic Saline (Muro 128) 5% drops (4x/day) and ointment (qhs)
Warm air (hair dryer at arm's length) to increase tear evaporation
Lower IOP to reduce stromal hydrostatic pressure (Brimonidine/Timolol)
Bandage Contact Lenses (BCL) for pain management in ruptured bullae
Avoid Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors (CAIs) if possible (may inhibit endothelial pump)

sections.title: Surgical Complications
content: Graft Detachment (Most common; requires rebubbling)
Primary Graft Failure
Secondary Glaucoma (Steroid-induced or Pupillary block)
Iatrogenic Iris Damage / Uveitis
Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) - higher risk in triple procedures

content.explanation: P: Polymegathism (CV >40%); U: Under-count (CD <1000); M: Morphology change (Pleomorphism); P: Pump Failure (Edema)

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: DSO (Descemet Stripping Only): Stripping 4mm central zone without graft; relies on peripheral cell migration.
ROCK Inhibitors (Ripasudil/Netarsudil): Enhance endothelial cell proliferation and migration post-DSO.
ZEB1 and TCF4 studies: Linking specific CTG repeat lengths to surgical prognosis.
Pre-loaded DMEK grafts: Reducing intraoperative manipulation and improving tissue viability.
Endothelial Cell Injections: Cultured cell therapy (pioneered by Kinoshita et al.) showing promise in trials.

sections.title: Emergency Signs & Red Flags
content: Sudden ocular pain with redness (Ruptured Bulla / Infection)
Halos + Nausea + Fixed mid-dilated pupil (Acute IOP spike/Pupillary block)
Rapid drop in vision post-EK (Graft detachment/Rejection)
Stromal infiltrate (Secondary Microbial Keratitis)

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always perform Specular Microscopy before cataract surgery if guttae are present.
The 'Triple Procedure' is often preferred to avoid two separate surgeries.
In DMEK, the 'S-stamp' or 'F-mark' helps ensure proper orientation (Endo down).
Guttae are not always pathognomonic for Fuchs if they are purely peripheral (Hassall-Henle).
Post-op steroids must be tapered slowly to prevent rejection, especially in DSAEK.
